source.title: Deeply Explain CNN Via Hierarchical Decomposition
source.authors: Ming-Ming Cheng; Peng-Tao Jiang; Linghao Han; Liang Wang; P. Torr

record.file_problem: The text is complete. The supplied venue is International Journal of Computer Vision, while the paper text header says IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence.
record.tranche_reason: It measures how often channels from different CNN stages contribute to decisions across labeled categories, using a category-discriminativeness measure rather than directly testing neuron responses to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The study reports channel discriminative degrees by model, dataset, and stage in Fig. 14, and explicitly says low-level channels commonly activate for multiple categories while high-level channels are more discriminative. The figure provides no readable numeric values. Other results on gAP accuracy, saliency sanity checks, and classification performance do not measure polysemanticity and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: This is an attribution-method paper proposing gAP and hierarchical decomposition; it never measures polysemanticity. It cites Zoom In only for the importance of feature relationships. Its 'discriminative degree' (Eq. 13) counts how often a channel ranks top-3 in contribution across class labels. That is a class-selectivity score of decision contribution, not whether a neuron responds to several unrelated features. Low-level channels being shared across categories reflects generic edge or blob features, which no version treats as polysemanticity. The finding belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record overweights a side analysis. The authors mainly conclude that gAP efficiently and accurately decomposes CNN decisions into hierarchical channel-level evidence (high correlation with ablation ground truth, passes sanity checks) and helps diagnose failures and adversarial attacks. The channel discrimination analysis is a secondary observation, presented as consistent with Zeiler & Fergus: low-level features are shared and high-level ones are more discriminative.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses gradient-based activation propagation and category-level discriminative-degree analysis, not the neuron visualization or feature-interpretation procedure in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported channel discriminative degree changes across network stages; the text also reports differences among architectures, with deeper ResNet-50 high-level stages more discriminative than VGG-16 and AlexNet.

fits_no_version.finding: Channel discriminative degree (share of top-3 contribution counts from the most frequent class) is low in early stages and higher in late stages. In late stages it orders ResNet-50 > VGG-16 > AlexNet, on ImageNet and PASCAL VOC (Fig. 14, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Class-selectivity of CNN channels' decision contributions increases with depth and with architecture depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Many high-level channels have overlapping activation maps (IoU>0.9) for the same decision. The authors read this as representations distributed across channels (Fig. 6, Sec. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concepts in high-level CNN layers are distributed across multiple channels with redundant effects.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says source code and an interactive demo will be made publicly available.
record.peer_reviewed: International Journal of Computer Vision (venue metadata; paper text header says IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence)
record.problems: The category-discriminativeness measure does not show whether categories or inputs are unrelated, or identify a coherent semantic job for an individual channel. Fig. 14 supplies no readable numerical values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No results measuring the claim were left out. Other reported results, including gAP correlation with channel ablations, randomization sanity checks, surrogate-model accuracy and adversarial-response analyses, measure attribution-method performance or other behaviors rather than polysemanticity.
record.verdict_notes: The study never uses the terms polysemantic or superposition. Reader-assigned V1/V6 links and limits_scope labels are removed, since a category-sharing measure of contribution rank cannot show unrelated mixtures or misread generalization. Venue discrepancy noted: the header says TPAMI.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures category-level channel selectivity, not whether the inputs are semantically unrelated or whether a particular channel responds to specific unrelated images or concepts.
Language models and transformer MLP neurons.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Whether polysemanticity arises from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
SoLU, modern convnet design or regularization changes to polysemanticity, and whether it can be reduced without performance loss.
The study does not identify the semantic function of specific apparently mixed channels or test whether their category responses share one coherent feature.
How activation-range choice or explanation scoring affects polysemanticity judgments.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Measured channel discriminative degree across categories using the share of top-three channel contributions assigned to the most frequent category.
rows.measure: Channel discriminative degree; lower values indicate channels selected across categories more evenly.
rows.note: The text describes low-level channels overall as having small discriminative degrees and responding across categories, but the plotted value is not given numerically and does not establish that the category inputs are unrelated.
rows.check: Class-level contribution selectivity, not response to unrelated inputs; figure-only value. Applies identically to r1–r30.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Channel discriminative degree across stages and the tested ImageNet and PASCAL VOC settings
reader_labels.reason: The reported category-level selectivity differs by depth: low-level channels are described as responding across categories, while high-level channels are more discriminative; the measure does not establish unrelatedness. Rows r1-r30.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Channel discriminative degree across stages and the tested ImageNet and PASCAL VOC settings
reader_labels.reason: The results are consistent with low-level category-general features and greater high-level category discrimination, but do not establish that specific mixed-response channels have one coherent semantic job. Rows r1-r30.
